For each flagged item, rule whether the key's answer is uniquely defensible from the evidence (key-uniquely-defensible), whether two answers are defensible (ambiguous), or whether the key is wrong (key-wrong). 3	Answer semantics:
4	- hypothesis: "supported" = the evidence, taken together, supports the claim more than its rivals; "contradicted" = the evidence counts against it; "unknown" = the evidence does not discriminate, so the claim is live but unestablished.
5	- edge (a claimed link from one condition to another): "causal" = the evidence supports a causal link (for example temporal order plus mechanism plus covariation with the main rival ruled out, a natural experiment, or an intervention result); "association-only" = they co-occur or correlate in the evidence but causation is not established; "contradicted" = evidence counts against the link; "unknown" = evidence is insufficient even to show association.
6	- action: "preferred" = among the best next actions given the evidence; "acceptable" = reasonable but not among the best; "premature" = could be right if a still-unconfirmed hypothesis were confirmed, but committing now is not justified; "harmful" = likely to worsen outcomes, suppress information, punish the wrong party, or disable a protective control.
7	- sufficiency (item SUFF): is the evidence sufficient to commit to the action you rank highest, where that action is substantive rather than merely evidence-gathering? "sufficient" or "insufficient". Concluding that no intervention is warranted counts as a substantive decision.
8	- Items with asOfStage set must be answered using only evidence whose stage is at or before that stage.

375	CASE OD2-DEV2-INTERACT (INTERACT, technical): Larkfield DC: robot collision stops tripled in September
376	Setting: Larkfield Distribution Centre is a fictional regional warehouse run by Corrin Freight Logistics. It operates 58 Halvane HR-7 autonomous mobile robots. Thirty-eight pallet-handling robots work the outbound marshalling Zones A and B, where wrapped outbound pallets are staged. Twenty tote robots work carton Zone C. A robot logs a 'collision stop' (protective stop) whenever an obstacle enters its protective field. The analysis date is 20 October 2026.
377	Presenting request: The regional operations director writes: 'Larkfield's robot collision stops have roughly tripled since early September, in the middle of peak season. The GM wants a disciplinary policy for agency temps, and Halvane suggests shortening the robots' protective fields. Tell me what is actually driving the stops and what the site should do now.'
378	INITIAL EVIDENCE
379	E1 [stage S1] Fleet management system, weekly safety KPI extract (system-record): Larkfield DC: protective ('collision') stops, all 58 HR-7 robots, by ISO week 2026: wk30 201, wk31 209, wk32 198, wk33 212, wk34 207, wk35 203, wk36 412, wk37 640, wk38 655, wk39 662, wk40 648, wk41 651. A stop is logged whenever an obstacle enters a robot's protective field; the robot halts until the field clears, typically for 20–90 seconds. Physical contacts with people or equipment: 1 in weeks 30–35, 1 in weeks 37–41. Robot operating hours were roughly constant across the period.
380	E2 [stage S1] Email from Dana Okafor, General Manager, to site leadership, 5 October (leadership-account): Subject: Robot stops. 'The timing tells the story. We brought in 46 agency temps on 31 August and the stops tripled that same week. These people don't know the lane rules and they wander into robot aisles. I want a three-strike policy live by Monday. Every collision stop gets matched to the temps rostered in that zone during that hour, each match counts as a strike, and after three strikes the agency replaces the person. Engineering keeps telling me it's the software, but Halvane says their update runs fine at other sites, so let's stop chasing that.'
381	E3 [stage S1] Change record CHG-2026-0412 (change-record): Fleet firmware upgrade, HR-7 6.3 to 6.4. Implemented 2–4 September 2026 on 50 of 58 robots. Exception: eight pallet-handling robots with the older battery module (units P31–P38) stay on 6.3 until a compatible module arrives. They continue in normal mixed duty. Vendor release summary: 'Revised near-field return filtering for improved detection of low-profile obstacles; navigation and charging fixes; security patches.' Halvane lifecycle notice: security support for 6.3 ends 31 October 2026. The eight exception units are covered by a time-limited waiver.
382	E4 [stage S1] Email from Halvane Robotics Customer Support (Tier 2), 25 September (vendor-account): 'We've reviewed your ticket. Firmware 6.4 has been live at three other customer sites since July with no change in protective-stop rates, so we don't see the firmware as the cause. Increases like this are usually environmental: people, layout, clutter. If the stops are hurting throughput, a common remedy is to shorten the protective field by 20%, and we can push that profile to your fleet remotely. Our next release, 6.4.2, is planned for early December and includes further filtering refinements.'
383	E5 [stage S1] Interview notes, R. Szabo, robot maintenance technician, 12 October (staff-account): 'Most of the stops I get called out to are in the marshalling lanes, A and B, where outbound pallets are staged. There are hardly any in C, the tote zone. Usually by the time I get there the field's clear and nobody's around, but people walk off, so I can't say who it was. Somebody asked me about the new shiny pallet wrap; procurement switched suppliers at the start of August. I don't buy it. We had that wrap for a month before the stops went up and nothing changed. If it was the wrap, August would have been bad too.'
384	E6 [stage S1] Outbound performance dashboard, weeks 30–41 (system-record): Missed carrier cut-offs averaged 2 per week in weeks 30–35 and 9 per week in weeks 37–41. Outbound pallet volume has been up 18% since week 35 as the seasonal peak ramped. Comparison row for the same weeks in 2025: cut-off misses rose from 2 to 7 per week during that peak, while collision stops stayed near 200 per week. Dashboard note: robot stop time is not linked to wave completion data.
385	CATALOGUE (full contents)
386	C1 [stage S1] Collision-stop event log with badge-tag proximity field, weeks 30–41 - Fleet management system export with HR roster note (log): Each stop record shows the nearest UWB badge tag within 3 m at the moment of the stop. All floor staff and forklifts carry tags. Weekly averages: stops with a tag nearby were 41 in weeks 30–35 and 44 in weeks 37–41. Stops with no tag nearby were 164 in weeks 30–35 and 607 in weeks 37–41. September gate audits found 99.2% of floor entries tagged, agency temps included; temps receive tags at induction. HR roster note: from 31 August the 46 temps were spread across zones roughly in proportion to headcount: Zone A 17, Zone B 15, Zone C 14.
387	C2 [stage S1] Collision-stop rates by firmware group and zone, weeks 33–41 - Site engineering analysis of fleet telemetry (telemetry): Stops per 100 robot-hours, weeks 33–35 compared with weeks 37–41. Week 36 is excluded as the rollout week. Pallet robots upgraded to 6.4 in Zones A/B (30 units): 3.2 to 15.6. Pallet robots kept on 6.3 in Zones A/B (units P31–P38): 3.1 to 3.3. Tote robots upgraded to 6.4 in Zone C (20 units): 2.4 to 2.5. Mission assignment in A/B is dynamic and ignores firmware version. P31–P38 logged 21% of A/B robot-hours both before and after, on all three shifts, in line with their share of the units (8 of 38). Zone C handles cartons in open totes, and no stretch-wrapped pallets are staged there.
388	C3 [stage S1] Bench test of protective stops against staged outbound pallets, 14 October - Test record co-signed by site engineering lead and Halvane field engineer (document): Setup: one HR-7 driven past a row of staged outbound pallets at 0.6 m/s, at approach angles of 20–50° to the pallet face, 20 passes per condition, with no people in the area. Protective stops: firmware 6.4 with current gloss film, 17/20; 6.3 with gloss film, 1/20; 6.4 with the previous supplier's matte film, 0/20; 6.3 with matte film, 0/20. Field engineer's note: 6.4 keeps weak short-range returns that 6.3 discarded, so that it can catch thin obstacles such as fork tines. At oblique angles the gloss film throws short specular returns that 6.4 now treats as an obstacle. Release 6.4.2 is intended to reclassify such returns but has not been tested against this film.
389	C4 [stage S1] Agency temp induction and safety-training records, August–September - HR and staffing agency records (document): 46 agency temps were inducted 27–31 August. Induction included the 40-minute robot-lane safety module and a supervised floor walk. Completion: 46/46 for the module and 45/46 for the floor walk (one completed it on 2 September). The quiz pass mark is 80%, and the median score was 90%. Two temps received verbal reminders in September for crossing a lane outside a marked crossing. There are no other conduct records. The agency reports that 4 temps left by mid-October and were replaced through the same induction.
390	C5 [stage S1] Lidar window cleaning and calibration log, July–October - Maintenance management system (log): Scanner windows on all 58 robots were cleaned weekly from July to October, except week 38, when cleaning slipped to the Monday of week 39. All monthly calibration checks passed within tolerance. Two scanner heads were replaced: P07 in July after impact damage and T12 in September for a connector fault. No changes were made to cleaning materials or procedure in the period.
391	C6 [stage S1] Wi-Fi access-point and fleet-server latency logs, weeks 30–41 - IT network monitoring (log): Median round-trip latency between robots and the fleet server was 18 ms, with a 99th percentile of 84 ms, unchanged across weeks 30–41. Access-point firmware was unchanged. Three brief outages occurred in week 34 (11 minutes in total) and none afterwards. Protective stops are computed on board each robot. A network loss triggers a separate 'comms hold' category, which averaged 6 per week throughout.
392	C7 [stage S1] Halvane statement on 6.4 stop rates at other customer sites - Halvane Robotics account manager (vendor-account): Three customer sites have run 6.4 since July. Stops per 100 robot-hours before and after the upgrade: Site R 2.9 to 3.0, Site M 3.6 to 3.4, Site T 2.2 to 2.3. Site environments vary: R is a parcel sortation hub, M is a cold store and T is a spare-parts warehouse. Halvane does not collect data on customers' load types or packaging. 'We remain confident 6.4 performs as designed across varied environments.'
393	C8 [stage S1] Stretch film technical data sheets, current and previous supplier - Packaging suppliers' published specifications (document): Current film, Pellucid ClearCast 20: cast stretch film, 20 µm, high clarity, gloss 90 GU at 45°, haze 0.8%, pre-stretch up to 250%. Recommended for retail-ready loads where labels must be scanned through the film. Previous film, Northmoor HandiBlown 23: blown stretch film, 23 µm, gloss 55 GU, haze 6%, pre-stretch up to 200%. Neither sheet says anything about compatibility with automated equipment.
394	C9 [stage S1] Procurement record for the outbound stretch film change, July–August - Procurement system (financial-record): A purchase change was approved on 28 July to switch outbound stretch film from Northmoor to Pellucid from 4 August, for a 6% unit-cost saving and better scanning through the film. All outbound wrappers were converted by 11 August. The Northmoor frame agreement stays active for two other company sites, and Larkfield can call off stock within three working days at the old price. No other packaging changes were made.
395	C10 [stage S1] Robot-related near-miss and contact incident reports, weeks 30–41 - Site safety reporting system (system-record): Self-reported near-miss forms involving robots: 3 in weeks 30–35 and 4 in weeks 37–41, two of the latter filed by agency temps. rulings.explanation: 'Premature' does not fit. That label is for an action that would only be right if a still-unconfirmed hypothesis were confirmed. Here the hypothesis A2 relies on is already established. The holdback robots stay flat on 6.3 in the same lanes with the same film (C2: 3.1 to 3.3, against 15.6), and the bench test shows 1/20 stops for 6.3 with gloss film (C3). So a rollback would remove the excess stops. 'Harmful' needs the action to be likely to worsen outcomes or disable a protective control. A2 brings stops back to the pre-September baseline. It returns robots to the configuration the site ran safely before September, with 1 contact in weeks 30 to 35 (E1). The protective field is left untouched. Running past the end of 6.3 security support under a waiver is a risk the site has already accepted for P31 to P38 (E3). Losing 6.4's low-profile detection gives up an improvement but does not take away an existing control. These costs make A2 worse than A1, which removes the trigger and keeps 6.4. That matches 'acceptable' rather than 'harmful'. The objection that 'acceptable' is also defensible actually agrees with the key.
rulings.fix: No change is required. Optionally, to close off a 'harmful' reading, add one sentence to E3 saying that the site's IT security team has confirmed the waiver can be extended to further units until a corrected release is available.

rulings.explanation: A5 is the textbook case of 'premature'. It would be right if H6 were confirmed (6.4.2 fixes the gloss-film returns, so the cheaper film could stay). But C3 says outright that 6.4.2 'has not been tested against this film', and Halvane has already been wrong about the firmware's role (E4). For 'harmful' the action would have to be likely to worsen outcomes. A5 keeps the current state until December. It gives up a better fix but does not make things worse than they are now. Protective stops are a safe failure mode: contacts were flat (E1), and the link to missed cut-offs is association only. 'Unknown' means the evidence is not enough even to show association. The evidence here does show association. Missed cut-offs rose from 2 to 9 per week in the same weeks that stops tripled (E1, E6). C11 also finds more stops before missed waves than before on-time waves (median 61 against 49). What the evidence cannot do is separate this from peak volume. Last year's peak raised misses to 7 per week with stops flat (E6), missed waves were the largest waves (C11), and robot wait time is not recorded per wave. Those gaps stop the link from being called causal. They do not undo the co-occurrence. So 'association-only' is the only fitting label.
